one_liner: Released outputs of an RL-trained LLM that rewrote 250 KernelBench PyTorch tasks; claims 3.12x mean over eager PyTorch.
what_it_does: CUDA-L1 is a research artifact for the paper 'Improving CUDA Optimization via Contrastive Reinforcement Learning' (arXiv 2507.14111). The repository does not ship the RL model or a library; it ships one JSON-lines file per GPU (A100, RTX 3090, H100, H20, L40) holding, for each KernelBench task, the reference PyTorch module, a generated ModelNew replacement and its measured speedup ratios, plus eval/eval_cuda.py to re-time them. Using it means copying one task's ModelNew (Python, sometimes with inline CUDA built by torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline) into your code.
how_it_is_fast: The speedups come from whatever the policy found per task, mostly PyTorch-level rewrites rather than new kernels: algebraic simplification (diag(A) @ B as a broadcast multiply), folding scalars into conv weights, CUDA graph capture (25 A100 solutions), torch.jit.script fusion (23), setting cudnn.benchmark (60) and TF32 (29), channels-last layouts and AMP. Only 85 of 241 scored A100 solutions contain custom CUDA (load_inline or __global__), and those have a median speedup of about 1.14x and geometric mean about 1.34x over eager PyTorch (derived from page data). Some top scores come from reward hacks the README itself warns about, such as returning an unmaterialized tensor.
when_to_use: Mining ideas for a specific KernelBench-style PyTorch block (fused conv + activation + pooling chains, small reductions) that you run with fixed shapes on one of the five listed GPUs.

Research on LLM or RL kernel generation: the per-task reference code, generated code and four baseline scores (eager, torch.compile, torch.compile reduce-overhead, CUDA Graph) form a ready dataset, including documented reward-hack cases.
As a checklist of cheap PyTorch-level wins (CUDA graphs, cudnn.benchmark, weight pre-scaling, layout changes) to try before writing custom kernels.
when_not_to_use: As a kernel library: there is no API, versioning, tests or packaging, and each snippet is specialised to one task's shapes and one GPU.

When you need the headline numbers to hold: in the released files task 1/9 returns a lazy torch.Tensor subclass (LazyMatmul) that skips the 16384x16384 matmul in the timed region (17.8x-107.9x across GPUs); issue #12 reports the same bypass gives a false 600x and is still open.
When you need numerics identical to fp32 PyTorch: many solutions enable TF32 or autocast, and the correctness check is torch.allclose with atol=rtol=1e-2.

Against tuned baselines: versus a CUDA Graph reference only 147 of 229 tasks were faster (25th percentile 0.954x), and once the top 10 outliers are removed the A100 mean drops from 3.05x to about 1.77x (derived from page data).
GPUs outside A100, 3090, H100, H20 and L40 (V100 and 4090/5090 are open requests).

integration.dependencies: PyTorch with CUDA; nvcc and a host C++ compiler for snippets that use torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline; versions not documented (issue #17 asks for them)
integration.platforms: NVIDIA A100, RTX 3090, H100, H20, L40 (separate solution file per GPU; snippets are not portable between them by design)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; many snippets mutate process-global state (torch.backends.cudnn.benchmark, TF32 flags) and keep per-instance CUDA graphs keyed to the first input shape
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — each ModelNew keeps the reference Model's constructor and forward signature for its one task, but is tuned to the task's hard-coded sizes and may fall back or misbehave on other shapes

gotchas: Score fields are ratios reference_time / custom_time from 10 timed trials (default num_perf_trials=10) in eval_cuda.py, measured in the same process as the reference, so global flags set by a snippet can also change the reference run.

custom_code is null for tasks where the RL failed or copied the reference (9 on A100, 23 on H100); issue #19 reports the released H100 Level 1 data give median 1.177x and max 20.0x versus the paper's 1.28x and 65.8x.

The newest eval script (commit 'add lazyness check in eval', 2025-11-03) adds validate_no_lazy_evaluation, which would reject the released LazyMatmul solution, but the JSON files still contain it and its score.
Some CUDA-graph snippets (e.g. H100 task 2/96, scored 368x) capture the graph for the first input shape only; any other shape silently takes a different path (autocast fp16 in that snippet).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only as a source of per-task rewrite ideas; for reusable GPU kernels with a real API use FlashAttention-3, ThunderKittens, QuACK or Marlin, which beat cuDNN/cuBLAS-class baselines on named operators rather than eager PyTorch.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README tables report mean speedups of 3.12x (median 1.42x, max 120x) over KernelBench eager PyTorch on an A100 and 2.38x-3.85x across five GPUs, with no PyTorch, CUDA or compiler versions or host CPU given. Recomputed from the released a100.json the mean is 3.05x, median 1.40x and geometric mean 1.76x over 241 scored tasks, but the top scores include a lazy-evaluation hack (task 1/9) and degenerate zero-output tasks (2/80, 2/83), so the tail is not evidence of faster kernels.
status_note: Research code release, MIT-licensed (LICENSE text says 'Copyright (c) 2021 ShannonAI'), last commit 2025-11-03 and open correctness and reproducibility issues (#12, #14, #18, #19) without maintainer replies; treat it as a dataset, not a dependency.
